blocks.prompt: The Pirate Ship That Voted
blocks.text: Pirate ships were not big. Most pirates picked a small ship called a sloop. A sloop was quick. It could turn fast. It could slip into shallow water where big navy ships could not go. The crew did not have a boss who yelled at them. The crew voted. They picked their own captain. If they did not like him, they voted for a new one. Every pirate got a share of what the ship took. The cook got a share. The boy who climbed the mast got a share too.

blocks.prompt: Why Pirates Wanted Small Ships
blocks.text: In the movies, a pirate ship is a giant wooden castle with three tall masts and rows of cannons. Real pirates would have laughed at it. A big ship is slow. It needs a huge crew to sail it. It sits deep in the water, so it cannot follow anyone into a shallow bay. Most pirates chose a sloop instead. A sloop was small, with one mast and one big sail. Twenty or thirty men could handle it. It could outrun almost anything afloat, and it could sail into water only a few feet deep. When a navy warship came hunting, the pirates simply steered somewhere the warship could not follow. Pirates also cleaned their ships far more often than the navy did. They ran the ship up onto a quiet beach, tipped it on its side, and scraped the weeds and barnacles off the bottom. This was called careening. A clean hull slides through water. A dirty one drags. That scraping was the difference between catching a ship and losing it.

4.title: The Pirate Ship That Voted
4.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for ages 9 to 10
4.intro: Read the passage, then answer in full sentences. Some questions ask what you think, not just what the passage says.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

blocks.prompt: The Rules Pirates Wrote for Themselves
blocks.text: Before a pirate crew sailed, they did something surprising. They sat down and wrote rules, then everyone signed them. These were called the articles, and they governed the ship. The articles of Bartholomew Roberts survive in print. They gave every man a vote in affairs of the moment. They gave every man an equal claim to fresh food and strong drink. They banned gambling with cards or dice for money, because crews that gamble start fights. Lights out at eight. Keep your weapons clean and ready. And if a man was crippled or lost a limb in the service, the articles paid him eight hundred dollars out of the common fund, with smaller injuries paid in proportion, before anyone else took a share. The captain was elected, and the crew could vote him out again. His absolute authority lasted only while chasing an enemy or fighting one. The rest of the time, the quartermaster ran the ship, settled arguments, and divided the loot. The captain took about two shares. An ordinary sailor took one. Compare that to the navy and the merchant ships those men had escaped from. A captain there was appointed, not chosen. He could order a sailor flogged. Wages went unpaid for years. A sailor crippled at work was put ashore with nothing. Pirates were thieves, and often violent ones. But on their own decks, in the 1720s, they were voting, sharing, and paying each other for injuries while most of the world did none of those things.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Edward Teach, known as Blackbeard

blocks.prompt: The Flag Was the Weapon
blocks.text: A cannon fight is a terrible way to steal a ship. Cannonballs smash the hull you wanted, kill the crew you might have recruited, and ruin the cargo you came for. A sinking prize is worth nothing. So the most successful pirates worked hard to never fight at all. Their main weapon was a flag. When a pirate ship closed on a merchant vessel, it ran up a black flag. The message was specific and well understood: surrender now and you will not be harmed. If the merchant refused, the black flag came down and a red one went up. Red meant no quarter. Nobody spared. Faced with that choice, most captains surrendered, and most pirate captures ended without a shot. Edward Teach understood this better than anyone. History remembers him as Blackbeard, and the beard was deliberate. Before boarding, he tucked slow-burning lengths of hemp cord under his hat and into his beard and lit them, so he arrived wreathed in smoke, hung with pistols, looking like something that had climbed out of the dark. Accounts of his career record remarkably little killing. He did not need to kill. His reputation did the work, and he built that reputation carefully, then spent it. His ship helped. In 1717 he took a French vessel, fitted her with about forty guns, and named her Queen Anne's Revenge. Forty guns made her a serious warship, and it was not a coincidence. A ship that looks unbeatable rarely has to prove it. The end came quickly. In 1718 the Queen Anne's Revenge ran aground at Beaufort Inlet in North Carolina and was abandoned. Blackbeard was hunted down and killed months later. His whole pirate career lasted about two years. In 1996 divers found a wreck in that inlet, buried under sand and cannons, and it is now widely accepted as his ship. Two years of work. Three centuries of fame. The flag really was the weapon.

6.title: The Pirate Ship That Voted
6.subtitle: A reading and history sheet for age 13
6.intro: Read the passage closely, then answer in full sentences. Cite the text directly where a question asks for evidence.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Golden Age of piracy: roughly 1650 to 1730
Roberts's articles gave every man a vote
800 dollars from the common fund for a lost limb
The captain held total power only in chase or battle
Walking the plank was invented by later writers
William Kidd is the rare documented treasure burial

blocks.prompt: The Democracy That Flew a Black Flag
blocks.text: Pirate ships were criminal enterprises. They robbed, they terrorized, and a good number of the men aboard them were violent. Hold that thought, because the rest of this is stranger than it sounds. In the 1710s and 1720s, a merchant sailor's life was close to unbearable. He was often pressed into service against his will. His captain was appointed by an owner he would never meet, and that captain's authority was total: he could order floggings, withhold food, and dock wages for damage. Pay arrived late or never. If a falling spar crushed the sailor's hand, he was set ashore with a useless arm and no money. There was no appeal, because the law was the captain. Now consider what those same men built when they stole a ship and sailed it for themselves. The first thing a pirate crew did was write rules and sign them. The articles of Bartholomew Roberts, which survive in print, open by granting every man aboard a vote in affairs of moment. Not the officers. Every man. The captain was elected by that vote and could be removed by it, and his absolute authority applied only in chase or in battle. Outside of combat, the crew's real executive was the quartermaster, whom they also elected, and whose job was to divide the plunder and settle disputes. The pay was startling. A merchant captain might earn many times his crew; a pirate captain took roughly two shares to an ordinary sailor's one. And the articles carried something no navy and no shipping company then offered: compensation for injury. Roberts's crew set aside 800 dollars for the loss of a limb, paid out of the common fund before any share was divided. That is a disability fund, drafted by thieves, roughly two centuries before most nations wrote one into law. Why did any of it hold? Not virtue. Structure. A pirate ship had no owner ashore to enforce a captain's will, no admiralty to appeal to, and no way to replace a crew that walked. Power sat with the men who could vote, and so the rules protected them. Fairness was not a value the pirates imported. It was the shape the situation forced. And the same clear-eyed logic ran through everything they did. They chose small sloops because small sloops were fast and could hide in shallow water. They careened their hulls obsessively because barnacles cost them speed and speed was survival. They flew a black flag offering safety in exchange for surrender, and a red one promising none, because a ship taken without a fight is a ship worth keeping. Almost nobody walked a plank; that image was invented later by writers. Almost nobody buried treasure either, William Kidd being the rare documented exception. Buried silver earns nothing. Spent silver buys another voyage. It is tempting to make heroes of them. Resist that. These were armed robbers, several of them slavers before and during their pirate careers, and their fairness stopped hard at the edge of their own deck. The point is not that pirates were good. The point is that when ordinary sailors were finally handed the power to design a workplace, they immediately designed votes, shared pay, and injury insurance. They knew exactly what was wrong with the world they had escaped. They had been telling us for years. Nobody was listening until they raised a flag.
